summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 In Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, (I) the Public Analyst had reported that the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and I am of the opinion that the same is adulterated due under section 2(1)(f). The Food Inspector reported that "Date of Analysis: 10 1 1969, Insect infestation" includes infestation even by dead insects, the further point to be considered is whether mere insect in infested form without more, would be sufficient to hold the article to be 'adulterated ' within the meaning of sub clause (f) of section 2 of the Act. If it is read conjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it, sub clause(f) with slight consequent rearrangement and parenthesis would read like this: "If the article is unfit for human consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it consists wholly orin part of a filthy, puttingrid, Disgustting, rotten or decomeased animalor or being insectable, (b) or on account for any other cause". To fall under that sub clause an article of food must be unfit for Human consumption because it consist wholly or partly in part and partly in parts of any obscene, put up with disgurbing, disagusting, rotting, decomposing or dishargustering, rotating or insect fested, it would be deemed to be unfitfor human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section2(1) (f). If the article was unfit for personal consumption on the account of the presence of the meal worms, the certificate of the Public analyst does not support the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi powder was either worm or infested or that on account Of any other reason" in association of what preceding it, the sample would be unfit to human consumption.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The defence of the appellant was that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother were in possession of 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other grains found in their pos session, were grown, 901 The defence was that the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn. Held: (i) It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to 'business as a trader and that is the essence of the Order. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He executed a number Of lease deeds, produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he had cultivated 80 90 bigha of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, we have to see whether they are genuine or not and Whether an inference of innocence can be based upon them. The total circumstances in the case show that the appellant is an agriculturist, and it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the land described in schedule to the plaint, on the terms of the Kabuliyat executed by the defendant on 24th December, 1924. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and after 1926 the defendant ceased to be a tenant from month to month under him and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 Of the Transfer o f Property Act. On the expiry of the second annual lease which happened on 7th December 1926, the defendant continued to remain a tenant in relation to the land in suit and no tenancy could be created by the two payments of rent, inasmuch as the Receiver had no authority to receive them. The plaintiff avers that by reason of the payment of rent on 8th March, 1925, and 16th March , 1926, he became a tenant and no new tenancy was effected by holdingover as is envisaged by section116 Of the Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926. Held, that the defendant 's tenancy was one from monthto month since its inception in 1924, and consequently a tenancy from month To month came into existence in accordance with the provision of section 116, Transfer of property Act, terminable by fifteen days notice. It would be pertinent to point out in tiffs connection that in the Second Appeal preferred by the plaintiff against the dismissal of his earlier suit by the lower appellate court, he admitted in his written statement that payment to him had the same effect as payment to the plaintiff and the trial judge took the same view as was taken by the High Court on the previous occasion, that by payment and acceptance of rent a new tenancy created de hors the Kabiuliyat, and as the new tenancy came into force in accordance With the provision Of section 116 Transfer of the Property Act even though No rent was demand ed by the tenant after 1926, such acceptance amount ed to his assenting to the continuing in possession is evidenced by acceptance of rents from him in the year 1926.

The Income tax Officer issued a notice to the assessee under section 138(1)(b) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 on April 1, 1964 asking him to produce documents in support of his claim for privilege under section 139(1) (b) and to furnish the sought for information thereafter as to the amount of tax determined, as payable by an assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 on or before April 1. 1964, and authorised the Commissioner to furnish or cause to be furnished the sought information, if he was satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. The assessee contended that after the repeal of section 137 of the 1961 Act by Act V of 1964, there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of documents from the income tax authorities after April 1 1964 relating to assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(I)(b), had no relationship to the power of the court to summons that record. The High Court dismissed the assessee 's appeal holding that the omission of section 138 did not make any difference and that in view of the repeal, there was no longer no impediment left for the exercise of powers by a court to summoning the production or the disclosure of any information therefrom to it, in a case pending before the court when the court, by a judicial order, requires the production Of the record considered relevant by it for decision of a case instituted before it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 139(I) does not affect the powers of the courts to require production of assessment records from the Income tax authorities subsequent to April 1 1966 relating to the assessment proceedings for 1964 65 in respect to the record filed after April1, 1964 relating only to assessment year 1964 65. The finality attached thereto is, thus restricted to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person other than a court of law by a Judicial order. [558G H] (2) The finality which has been attached to the order of Commissioner under section138(1), is, therefore, limited to the case where theinformation etc. are called for in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the commissioner of Income Tax, it would have said so in Section 138 of the Act itself. [559G H; 559A] (3) The High Courts fell in error in holding that section 137 did not apply to the facts and circumstances of this case.

A gift by the husband to his minor wife to Seinaba was valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of his property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor. In the present case there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammotty and as the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. Possession was not delivered to Seinsaba but to her mother, the first appellant, and she accepted the gift on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband could receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; A gift to a minor was completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the property of the minor Wilayat ul Mal. The gift was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammottty to his mother in law and accepted by her on behalf, of the minors. In this case there is no legal guardian or of property in existence, the gift can be completed by delivery of the properties to and acceptance by any person in whose control the minor is at the time when the donor is himself the guardian or the de facto guardian or 'quasi guardian ' provided there was real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee, and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment was sufficient evidence of such an intention. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gifted for his benefit is the sole consideration. Mammosty was living at the house of her mother in Law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who was also residing with him, was capable under Muhammadan law to accept the gift and the minor was within the care either of the mother or of other near relative or even a stranger.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides that every religious institution, the annual income of which, for the fasli year immediately preceding as calculated for the purposes of the levy of contribution under sub section (1), is not less than one thousand rupees, shall pay to the Commissioner annually such contribution not exceeding five per centum of its income as the Commissioner may determine. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. Under section 76(2) of the Act audit fee is not to be prescribed by rules : the Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed) for meeting the cost of audit of the institution. That im.plies that the Commissioner had to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of accounts of the religious endowment, and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. The High Court was of the view that under the Act the Government had to make under section 100 rules applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution find no support in the provisions of the act or its scheme. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered; and (ii) that the audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The Commissioner had not determined the audit fees under section 76 of the Madras Act 19 Of 1951. He has to form a estimate of reasonable cost incurred in rendering an effective Audit of accounts for each religious endowment. [924 F H] (2) Under section 77(2), the audit shall be made (a) in the case of a religious institution the annual Income of which calculated as aforesaid for the Fasli year immediately previous is not higher than one hundred rupees, by auditors appointed in the prescribed manner; and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The Commissioner has also to form estimate of its reasonable cost for making an efficient audit of its accounts.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 2nd April, 1975 of the High court directing the issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt of the Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 19(1) of the Act from an order issuing notice as nothing yet has been decided by the High Courts. In appeal to this court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an appeal does lie to this Bench as a question of right from any kind of order made by the Court in the proceeding for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order merely initiating the proceedings without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right tinder section 19. In a given case special leave may be granted under article 136 of the Constitution from an Order initiating the proceeding. What is decided therein is this : that on a reference made by a Advocate General if the Court declines to take cognisance and to initiate proceedings for contempt, the order is not an order initiating contempt proceeding. The matter has to be decided either finally or may be. even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide some bone of contention raised by the alleged contemnor asking the High, Court to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section 20 of the . [501B C] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court,(1) Where the order or decision is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Supreme Court, such appeal shall lie to the Supreme court. But there are no observations by this Court nor on the facts of that case there can be any,. to show that an Appeal would lie to, this Court from an earlier order if the order does decide (1 ) A.I.R. , and (2) unless and until there is some order or direction of the court adjudicating upon any matter raised before it by the parties affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice is not appealable. [502C D] Barabakanta Misra vs Orissa State High Court, ; , referred to.

In a proceeding under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decree holder was in fact a benamidar for another person in respect of the decree, does not come within the purview of these provisions. If the purchaser is the decreeholder, himself and he is in possession of the property when the decree is reopened, it would be incumbent upon the court, to order restoration of those properties to the judgment debtor under clause (c) of section 36(2). In other words, the court has to order the payment of the decretal amount in such instalments as it thinks proper and cl. (e) further imposes a duty on the Court to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment Of any one of the instalments, the properties restored to the decree debtor under cl.(e) would be put back into the possession of 'the judgment debtor. The order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below should stand and set aside the order for restoring possession made in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that (i) even if Aghore was proved to have advanced the money upon which the Chakrabortys obtained the decrees, in reopening the decrees and in working out the rights of the parties in accordance with the provisions of the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Calcutta Money Lender Act, the Court could treat the Chakraborty as the decreeholders; (ii) even assuming that Aghorore was not proved to be a benamidars for her husband Aghoria, it was incumbent upon him to satisfy the court that the decree holders on record were in fact benamidars and (iii) in making a new decree under cl.(b) of sub section (2), the court can at all enter into the question as to who the decree debtors on record was himself a benamirer for another. HELD : (i)(a) The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of the decrees to the Judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled and in case of default in payment of any one instalment, the property is returned to the Decreeholder purchaser. It is quite true that the object of restoration possession of these properties in favour Of Oramba Sundari, the appellant has been held by both both the Courts below to be the purchasers of these lands within the meaning of clause (b) Of section 36; and as the subsequent conveyance of these property in favour orambaundari did not bona fide acquire any right which could be protected under clause(c), of section36(2), it was imperative upon the Court, to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act. The decreeholders, therefore, must be deemed to have been the purchasers and there is no proof of the orderholders being in possession, of the same either by themselves or through Oramb Sundari. In these circumstances, clause (e), of s 36(1) cannot be attracted in favour to judgment debtors so far as this property is concerned and the possession must remain with the appellant and there was no proof that they were in possession on the same day when the decrees were reopened. [163 F G] (ii)(a). In making a fresh decree under clause.(b), the Court can at any stage enter into such question as it considers necessary to give an order in such case that if the default in paying any one or of the instalment instalments, is made out, then the properties restore to the judgement debtor under clauses (c), (e).

The appellant was a transferee of the decree passed by the City Civil Court, Bombay. The transfer in writing of a property which is the subject matter of a suit without in terms transferring the decree to be passed in the suit in relation to that property does not entitle the transferee to apply for execution of the said decree as a transferee or a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that the language of Order XXI, rule 16 (old section 232) cannot be construed so as to apply to a case where there was no decree in existence at the time of assignment and this position was in effect conceded by Dixit J. and by the Division Bench when they observed that on a strict construction of the document in question amounted to a transfer or an agreement to transfer the decree, that as the decree was not transferred or agreed to be transferred to the respondent company by the document under consideration and the latter cannot claim to be transferees of the original decree by an assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XX, r. 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure, there is nothing in the provisions of order XXI, Rule 16 which prohibits him from availing himself of section 146 if the provisions Of that section can be availed of by him. The respondent company filed a suit for specific performance against the appellant on the ground that it was not in existence since at the date of assignment it operated as an agreement for transfer of the suit property when it would be passed, that such an agreement could be enforced by a suit of specific performance as contemplated by Order XXI Rule 16. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the document was not executed by Habib & Sons and (2) that there was nothing in Order XXI rule 16 which prohibited him from claiming the beneficial interest in the decree as an transferee of a decree by assignment in his writing within, the meaning Of Order XXI. HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 16 contemplates the actual transfer by an assignee in writing or by operation of law and enables such transferee to do it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. It is well settled that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name the property stands and Rule 10 enables the transferee of his decree to execute it in accordance with the same terms and conditions as the application for executing the decree has been passed and that while a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed therein, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transfereeof the decree by assign in writing. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, that its tender for providing and fixing " S.H. The respondent submitted that the contract with the Executive Engineers was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The Deputy Commissioner Excise & Taxation in appeal held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted : one for providing doors and windows in a specified building, and to promote sale of its manufactured goods undertook to fix the windows without demanding any charge for the service, and that the price of, the supplied but not the charge for service, was taxable. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the State of Rajasthan that the terms of the contract were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contracts as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the respondent. HELD : (i) The contract was a works contract and not a contract for sale. It may be a contract of sale where the main object is the transfer of the property in, and delivery of the possession of, a chattel as a chattels to the buyer. But if the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete, and, the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [508 G H] (ii) It was only upon the "fixing" of the window leaves that had become a part of the building construction that the property was to pass to the War Office under the head contract. But in both these cases, the Court held on a consideration of the terms and conditions of the agreement and the circumstances that the assessees had agreed to and did supply "motor bus being one for sale and not of service". [509 C D] (iii) It is only upon "fix" certain articles made by a manufacturer the contract must be deemed one for work and labour or one for the sale of a chatttel. The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials though not accessory to the execution of the works for a price; it may be contract for work in which the use of materials is 'accessory or incidental to the completion of the construction; or it may also be a contracts for work or use or supply of material although not accessory thereto to the execute of the same is voluntary or gratuitous. (iv) The test in each case is whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the chattelas passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to it, or it might be a Contract for work; or, it may, be acontract for work, in which case the property is to pass from the War office under the Head contract.

[280D] 3. It cannot be said that there is any infirmity in the judgment or order of a High Court as might induce us to interfere. The appeal fails and is dismissed. V.P .S. Appeal dismissed.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways he has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 and claims reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees appointing a fact finding Commission to inquire and report about the several train accidents from 1970 onwards and for several other directions to the State Government and the instrumentalities connected with the administration of the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. In view of the recent pronouncements of this Court no objection has been raised in the counter affidavit and we have not been called upon to adjudge the locus standi of the petitioner to maintain an action like this. As early as 1850 and three years before the opening of the first Railway track, Lord Dalhousie, the then Governor General of India had said in his minutes: "I trust they (the East India Company and the Government of India) will ever avoid the error of viewing Railways as private undertakings and will regard them as national works, over which the Government may justly exercise and is called uponto exercise stringent and salutary control This control should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or vexatiously exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the State and for the protection of the public. " The petitioner has maintained that he may every citizen of this country for the matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible; and that it is his duty to guard against attacks which may be more insiduous because they are novel and unprepared for. The quality of the service should improve. We do hope and believe that early steps shall be taken to implement in a phased manner the improvements referred to in the Counter affidavit and in our decision.

The appellants filed applications for restoration of the appeals before the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal under section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act. The application was dismissed by the Gujarat revenue Tribunal on July 18, 1961. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the application for restoration was made in time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear when the appeal or application was called for hearing, the Tribunal may restore the appeal and application to its file provided that where the other party had appeared in the appeal/ application such party shall be given notice and an opportunity of being heard before the order for resto ration of the appeal Or application is made. [144 H] (2) The words "decide it on merits" but in Regulation 20 the expression used is "decided ex parte" and we see no reason, either in the language or context of Regulation 20, why it should not include in its scope and ambit an application for restoring an appeal dismissed for nonprosecution as also an application to restore an appeal decided on merits under Regulation 19(1). If the view that the Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases was correct, it follows that Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period of limitation prescribed by that Regulation being 30 days from the date of receipt of such order, the applications were well within the period prescribed by Regulation 21.

The appellant 's case in the plaint was that Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village but also themselves dedicated the village Teli misconstru to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The trial court held that there was no absolute dedication of the village for the purpose of the temple by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was created thereby. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the Trial Court that dedication had not been proved but disagreeing with the trial court, it held that the plaintiff 's claim to succeed must be set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that by the Punch Faisala Award of 1796 an absolute dedication was made in favour of Shri Ramachandra Swamy temple or whether the village was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaran Lal absolutely with only a charge on it to meet the expenses of the Temple and did not make an absolute endowment of the property to the deity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i)(a) The document (the Panch Faishla Award) clearly shows an .absolute dedication of ' the village to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple for the general expenses of family or that he made certain alienations of the properties cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. It may well be that Ramsar Raman Lal was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family with only one charge on the property for the expenses for the temple and did Not make an express dedication of it to decide whether the Faisli Panchayati (i.e., award of panchas) was proper or not, adding that in case it was not proper, changes may be made in it whenever it may be necessary and improper. Even more important than that is the fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On the contrary, Mr. Bagchi accepted the previous award and gave his own interpretation of it, saying that by this Award Teliolera village was dedicated absolutely to the Temple of Shri Ramsaray Lal absolutely alongwith only a Charge on it for the expenditure of the family or, that he make certain alienations Of the property cannot change its absolute dedication from partial dedication into any partial dedication in respect thereof.

They did not justify the language of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, they are guilty of 'Criminal Contempt '; (ii) There is no gainsaying that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations. (iii) The High Court held that contemners Nos. 1 & 2 are guilty for contumacious behaviour and the High Court gave the ground that they had met and resolved that the ChiefJustice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he holds." Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In view Of the fact there is no gainaying that lawyers are the custodians of civilisation. Lawyers have to discharge their duties with dignity, decorum and discipline. [604B] (2) The language used by them was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act provides that a surety is entitled to the benefit of every security which the creditor has against the principal debtor at the time when the contract of guarantee was entered into, whether the surety knows of the existence of such security or not; and if the creditor loses, or without the consent of the surety parts with the other security, the surety is discharged to the extent of the value of the security lost as provided by section 141. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the specific understanding and with the full knowledge of the Bank that the principal borrower was offering another security, namely, pledge of goods and the goods were to be in the custody of the creditor Bank. In such a situation clause (a) of the explanation would be attracted and an application for restitution will have to be made to the Court of first instance, i.e. the Court Of Civil Judge Senior Division, Gondal. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debt pledging oil tins as and by way of security for the advance and, therefore, in view of combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of Indian Contract act, ( 'Act ' for short), the surety was discharged to it extent of value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost on account of the negligence of the principal creditor Bank, yet the surety would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: (1) In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee thereon on the good faith of other security being offered by the principaldebtor which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. [83G H] (2) In such an event clause (b) would be applicable and an Application for restitution would have to been made to Court of First instance, if it is held proved that security of pledged goods was lost at the date when the Contract of guarantee entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the guarantor knew of such other security offered by him, if the debtor knows of such another security offer by the surety, he may be discharged to that extent. [84G H; 85A B] (3) In a case where the suit in favour of the appellant and against the surety were decreed by the trial court, i e. the court of first example, and this decree has been reversed by the High Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction.

The appellant was the son of Amritrao, a member of the family of Amrit Rao. He claimed that as a result of this partition, the " patelki inam" lands were divided and the lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant. The trial court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regrant the land in accordance with the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 in force in Berar and section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928. On appeal, the High Court held that: (1)(a) the rights which the Rokade family had in these lands were rights of dealing with the property as owners, subject to a member Of the family rendering patel service; or in other words, the grant is a grant of land burdened with service and so long as the service is performed by any member of his family, the lands are joint family lands subject to partition, etc. among the members of the families, irrespective of whether he performs the service or not; (b) even if the aforesaid Rules and provisions applied, the appellant still retained his hereditary rights in the "patelki Inam" lands so long long as a member thereof works as patel; and (c) the orders of Government dated August 28, 1922, did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect of the " Patelki inams " lands and Government had no right to resume the same. Held:(i) The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules or the provisions Of the Patesls and patwaris law, 1900 applied; (ii) even assuming that the entire " p Patelki inam " lands in possession of Amritarao patel, including the plots which were made khalsa in 1904 05, were excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866, it was not open to Government to resume or regrant them to respondent No. 1; (iii) even though the appellant got possession by partition in 1923, it could only succeed if he establishes that he had a right to a share in the emoluments of the p Patel 's office and that Government has no right either to resume " P Patelki Inam lands and regadrant the same to respondent no. 1.

The appellant was a Cutchi Memon, and belonged to the same family as the other persons who had been made insolvents. He filed an application under section 64(1) of the , claiming that he was governed by the Hindu Law and stated that he rules of Hindu law applicable to cutchi Memons governed matters of succession and inheritance only. His contention was that as there was only one solitary decision of the High Court in favour of the respondents ' contention as against a large number of decisions of the Bombay High Court which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of inheritance, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. Held : (i) It is well settled that where the parties are governed in matters of pro perty, succession and succession by the rules of succession, including rules as to joint family property, their distribution according to the rule of survivorship and the right of a son in it by birth, the High court would be right in its view that the accountable persons having been born lone before 1948 had already acquired a right by birth in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act. (ii) It was not proved before him and never had been proved affirmatively that they had ever adopted as part of their customary law the Hindu law of be joint family as a whole or the distinction in that law between ancestral property as against self accquired property and the devolution thereof by survivorship, he held that the properties were governed by Hindu Law.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. It has, however, been held that if the purpose of removal of excisable goods is consumption in the same place where the excisable goods are manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods were used in the manufacture of any other commodity in the said place, this cannot be done without payment of excise duty at the place and in the manner prescribed. Thus if a commodity which is manufactured in such place or premises and is used for the manufacture or production of another commodity in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place and when the excisable product manufactured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture of another article in or outside such place, until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid at such place. In other words, if the commodity is taken inside the factory it will be removal and when excisable goods manufactured within the factory are removed from one plant to another it will not be a case of removal for the purpose Of payment of Excise duty. The Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49 provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or undertakings at an intermediary stage shall be treated as removed from any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured. Rule 9 provides that commodity obtained at intermediate stage of manufacture in a continuously process shall not be removed from the factory premises unless the excise duties leviable thereon have been paid on such goods at such places and in such manner as is prescribed in these Rules or as the Collector may require and except on presentation of an application in the proper form and on obtaining the permission of the proper officer on the form: " The remaining provisions of rule 9 which are not relevant for our purpose are omitted. ] 705 By a Notification No. " It has been already noticed that by section 5 1 of the Finance Act, 1982, amendments made to rules 9 and 49 have been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force, that is to say, from February 28, 1944 It is not disputed before us that under section 3(1) of the Act, the taxing event is the production or manufacture or of the excisable commodity at an earlier stage of an integrated process of manufacture of a new commodity by deeming such production or manufacturing of the commodity at any intermediate stage to be removal from such factory or premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) thereof. In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty on the yarn after it is sized for the purposes of weaving the same into fabrics. Be that as it may, as we have held that the commodity which was obtained at a intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process for weaving the said same into fabric, will be liable to payment of duty, the yarn that is produced by the appellants is also liable to excise duty.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1) (b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that since the interest of the remainder man may be prejudiced, the landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it is inherent in such a lifeinterest that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1)(b) as grounds for eviction by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others, who are not his tenants under the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenants are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and tenant when a suit is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the provisions of the Act. The question as has been sought to be established in the case by proving that there was no possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. On the other hand, the Act with regard to two different tenancies, though in the same premises, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose, is not maintainable. [275 D E] 2. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own ac count or on behalf, of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or be entitled to received the rent, if the building were let to a tenant". [275 F] 3. The definition of landlord is given in section 2 (6) to include the person receiving or has been entitled to receives the rent or be entitle to receive rent, whether on behalf or on his behalf, as an Agent, trustee executor, Administrator, receiver, or guardian, who would otherwise receive the same rent or he would so received the rents and profits of the premises. [276 B] 4. The words "landlord" in section 14 are wide enough to include a person who has been receiving or was entitled to receiving the rent for a building, whether in his own or on its behalf, and who admittedly had been on his personal right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the Premises from the tenants. [278 C] 5. The word "landlord is defined in section 3(7) as meaning any person who receives or is deemed to have received the whole or any part of the rent payable by him and includes a person entitled to get the rent if the premises were let for residential purposes, with right of sale, gift, etc., [278 D] 6.

In the appeals to this Court it was contended that even with respect to the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1967 68 the assessee did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coventry. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting adopted by the Income tax Officer for the relevant accounting years is really irrelevant. [105D] 1.2 In the circumstances of the case, it must be held that in the case of a non resident assessee like the petitioner clause (a) of sub section (2) of Section 5 has no application whatsoever and that Section 5(2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts on cash or mercantile basis. [106E] 1:3 The method adopted by an assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it was argued that if the assessee is proved to have maintained its accounts with respect thereto, then there is no receipt until it is received by it in U.K. Section 145 of the Act does amount to receipt of income by the assesee and is accordingly taxable and that it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in United Kingdom and not in India. [107E] In the instant case, the assessee was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (b) cannot apply. [108G H] 1 :4.1 Section 145 is relied upon by the Revenue to say that the method of accounts adopted by it for all its income is really relevant. In this view of the matter, it should be held in this case that the assessee had received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in UK. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Courtry. [109G H; 109A] 2.2 The method followed by the appellant for the accounting years 196768 68 and 1968 69 to the effect that it was maintaining its 106 accounts on mercantile basis, is really immaterial. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that the credit entry to the account of the assessee in the books of the Indian Company does amount not to receipt or receipt of any income by him. [110B] 2:3 In the present case, there is nothing to show that the money was not actually received, but the assessee firm was a creditor in respect thereof and unless it receives it in India, it could not have been said that it has received the amount. The argument is that the mere entry in the account books of Indian Company do not amount to its receipt by the petitioner and is therefore immaterial when does it actually receiving it in UK. [111A B] 2 :4 In the facts and circumstances of this case, we do not think it necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between Section 5 (2)(a) and Section 145 Of the Act nor is it necessary for express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that in this the case. the method adopted was really irrelevant and that section 5(3)(b), governs it regardless of the facts whether it maintained its account on cash support basis or mercantile foundation.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, their conviction under section 304 read with sections 149 and 147 was bad in law, because one or more of them might have participated in the commission of the offence and that in the present case on a fair reading of the entire judgment, it would be clear that the High Court found that though the charge as well as the evidence was directed against the 4 named accused, a court could come to the conclusion that the said person had a prior concert with one or other persons, named or unnamed, for committing the murder of the deceased in furtherance of their common intention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) When three of them were acquitted either on the ground that the evidence is not acceptable or by giving benefit of doubt to them, the result in law would be the same: it would mean that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the offence jointly with the acquitted persons. The effect of the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will be thesame : it would means that they do not conjointually act with the convicted accused. [608 G H] (2) When two or three persons convicted were acquitted both on the basis that the prosecution witnesses named only the said accused; but there may be other evidence, such as that given by the court witnesses, defence witnesses or circumstantial pieces of evidence, which may disclose the existence of named or nonexamed persons, other than those charged or deposed to by the prosecution witness, and the court, on the ' basis of the said evidence, may come to a conclusion that others, named and unnamed acted conjointly along with one of the accused charged. [613 B C] (3) The judgment of the High court cannot be sustained in law as it was contrary to the well settled principles laid down by this Court. It is not correct to say that when two or several persons convicted are acquitted, the court could convict a person under section302 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal code if it accepts the evidence that the accused acted in concert along with others named or omitted to take part in the offence. If that be so, before a court can convict a man under section 307, read with s 34, of the Code, it should come to an definite conclusion that one of them participated jointly in the committing of that offence. But evidence is adduced to prove that the persons other than the acquitted accused conjointly acted with the aid of the convicted person. [686 G H; 686 A B] (4) The charge discloses only named persons; it may also be that the prosecutions witnesses named merely the said two accused; and so have not been identified and so had not been named.

Section 15(1)(b) of the , provides that the rate of duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. Section 15(2) requires that the rates of duty, rate of exchange and tariff value, if so applicable, shall be determined according to the law prevalent on the day on which such goods were actually removed therefrom from the ware house. Sub section (3) provides that where a bill of entry has been present ed before the date of entry inwards of the vessel by which the import is made, the bill of Entry shall be deemed to have been presented on thedate of such entry in respect of such goods in accordance with the provisions of sub sections (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5). Section 15 provides that if a bill has been presented before the day of entry intowards of India by which goods are imported, the Bill of Entry may be deemed ted on the dates on which it was actually removedfrom the warehouse under section 68, on the said date. The petitioner 's case is that for the payment of duty the liability of the peti tioner to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. The respondents contended before this Court that the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the goods could not be released because of the prohibitory orders of the Income Tax Department under section 102 of the . Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right for the enforcement of which alone Article 32 of the Constitution is attracted. [655C D] 1.2 The petitioner as such has no fundamental fight to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. In a case of this type where liability depends on construction of law, and determination o f facts and th e provision of the particular statute FOR which elaborate procedures are pre scribed. It is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of fundamental right. When the order challenged is a valid and legal order, in spite of the allegation that it isGreater ous. I have, therefore, come to the conclusion that no question of the enforcement o f a fundamental fight arises in this case and the writ petition is not maintainable. [600E F] 1:3 In the instant case, it was found that as the goods were removed from warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come 627 into force, the customs authority and the Central Govern ment were right, in taking view that there was breach of the fundamental right which entitle a citizen for seek recourse to Article 32 Of the Constitution.

The appellants, who were the sons of a joint Hindu family, filed a suit for possession by partition of joint family property. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the whole estate including the share of the sons was sold in execution of the payment order and therefore the sale in execution could not be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father; that the sale could only be challenged on proof of the debt of defendant No. 1 which were characterised as misfeasance " and that the auction sale was under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code under which only "the right, title and interest of the defaulter" could be sold and therefore qua that property the sons had no interest left; and (6) that even if the debt was not avyavaharika the institution of the suit for partition operated as severance of status between the members of the family and therefore in an auction sale the share did not pass to the auction purchaser. Held, that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and (1) that whatever the nature of the debts, only the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end and consequently there was merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property by the sons which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to any end as a result of partition of the joint family properties. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration incurred as a consequence of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyayaharika debt as it cannot be termed " repugnant to good morals".

Rule 8(i) prescribes the method of payment of tax by means of stamps to be affixed to the tickets, and the second proviso is to the following effect: "Provided further that the tax payable under the Act on fare by the owner of a motor cycle rickshaw, rickshaw or a motor cab shall be paid to the State Government in lump sum, of which the amount shall be fixed by the State Govt from time to time by Notification in this behalf. Provided further that where the owner has not plied his vehicle for a continuous period of not less than three months and produces a certificate from the authority competent under the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act 1951 or the rules made thereunder to the effect that he has been refunded the tax for that quarter shall be payable by him immediately upon such cessation, and in case of such vehicles not registered in Rajasthan to the incharge of the check post or barrier at the time of their entry into the State of Rajasthan or to the officer of the Excise and Taxation Department nearest to the point of 523 entry into, the State and having jurisdiction over that area: Provided also that where a owner has failed to ply his vehicle on a date preceding any of the aforesaid dates, the proportionate amount for the quarter shall he paid by him forthwith upon such discontinuance, and (d) where the driver has not plying his vehicle within a continuous time of not more than three days and produces certificate from authority competent in that behalf to the effects that he had been refunded, the tax calculated on actual fares and freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan, or to, the officerof the Excise & Taxation Department nearer to the Point of 523 Entry into the States and having Jurisdiction over that territory: Provided further also that in cases covered by the second. proviso to sub rule (1) of Rule 8 and by subrule (ii) of that rule the lump sum fixed by a State Government as payable in lieu of the tax on fare or freight, as the case may be, shall be deposited in cash into a Government Treasury or a Sub Treasury in equal quarterly instalments payable within 15 days from the 31st day of March, the 30th day of September and the 31rd day of December every year. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of section 3 on the ground that it was violative of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The proviso to section 3 is extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax leviable on passengers and goods, though what it is to be is determined by the amount of fare orreight. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods transported by road or inland waterways" in section 3(1) are wide enough to include a tax which is not available to the state Legislature. (ii)(a) It makes the difference in the tax, and no case of discrimination can be said to be made out. The last contention is that the Act allows an option to pay a lump sum in lieu Of the tax but Rules 8 and 8 A and the notification make the payment of the lump sums compulsory.

The appellant was retrenched from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour Court directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The appellant challenged the award in this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In appropriate cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or discloses such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) (1). The only limited question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wages. Once leave against relief of reinstatement was rejected, the order of the Labour Appellate Tribunal holding that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstate must follow, has become final. [569D E] (2) The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this Court is whether even where reinstatement is found to be an appro priate relief, what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full or partial back wages, what can be the golden consideration for awarding Full and partial back Wages. Once Leave against relief is rejected, it becomes final. Article 136 of the Constitution does not envisage this Court to be a regular Court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal inter alia against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. Though Article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this Courtto exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made In violation of principles of Natural justice causing serious and grave hardship to parties and raise an important element of industrial Law requiring elucidations and final decisions by this court or disclosessuch other exceptional circumstances which warrant consideration of the Court ( See Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta vs their Workman).

At the suggestion of Nagju, Churi, Joginder and Nagju came to the house of the accused in village Shilaroo which is at a distance of 1 1/2 mile from Gani. The accused stated that he was with Churi in the house during the day but at 6 p.m. he left for Kotkhai leaving his wife alone at the house. It was also denied by the accused that his Kachha and coat were in a wet condition at the time of his arrest, As regards the 'blood stained Khokhri and shirt, the accused stated "I had cordial relations with my wife for the fast 14 years". According to the prosecution case, the injuries found on the body of Churi were caused by the appellant. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the evidence on record established beyond any manner of doubt that the accused suspected the fidelity of Churu deceased and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a result of his adulterous conduct; (2) there was nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder of Ch.uri deceased before the visit of the deceased to the residence of Shri Mahajan; and (3) the fact that the relations between the accused with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The evidence on the record establishes beyond any doubt that it was the accused and none else who caused injuries, to Chururi deceased as a consequence of which she died. It is also the case of the prosecution itself that shortly before the occurrence, the appellant enquired from the deceased regarding the father of the boy and the deceased thereupon abused him. The evidence establishes beyond all manner of doubts that the dead body was recovered after the accused had visited the house at about 10 p. m. while the intimation which was given by Mangat Ram (PW 10) to the police regarding a murderer having come to the place of occurrence was entered in the daily diary at 10.50 p.M. It would be difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child and it is difficult to belief that he will have insisted on Churi stayed with him after the child had visited his house. Had Joginder been the son of the respondent, the offence would have been committed during his absence cannot be accepted because there is nothing to indicate that the Police was aware about the murder before the visits of the victim to the House of the complainant to the accused. [14G H; 15A B] (ii) The statement recorded by the magistrate and signed by the complainant could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act, as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The appellant No. 1 was a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka Univer sity. The Govt. of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil), and (Mech.) for the Public Works Department. The selection was to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S (Direct Recruitment By Selection) Rules 1973. According to these rules total marks for qualifying examination were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus both the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State also submitted that there are many other candidates who had secured much higher marks than the appellant in case the above criteria is applied for selection. However, the Rules are clearly in violation of the dictum laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., J .T. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large Number of candidates have been selected though they had secured very high marks in the viva voce out of 50 marks kept for this purpose. Thus it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellant were bound by be selected on the ground of converting the same to 15%of the total Marks, the appellants before us were bound not be selected nor a large numbers of selected persons would have went much lower. In the light of the facts that appointments were made according to the rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However the Rules do not find it necessary to quash the selection on the above ground.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) In dealing with a case against an accused person, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a co accused person; it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. [413B C] (2) In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that she met her husband P.W.4 on that day. Adverse inference for not examining the wife has to be established and the chain has to been completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [414E F] (3) In the instant case, Sadanand had become entitled to the benefit of our doubts and his conviction is not sustainable.

The appellants were working as clerical and subordinate staff in the appellant 's concern. On a comparison of wages and dearness allowance prevalent in the four companies with wages 365 and dearness allowances prevalent in comparable concerns revised them, it was found that there were different scales of dearness allowance for clerical staff and other staff including factory workmen and the Tribunal therefore fixed the same rates on the same lines so that, so far as manufacturing concerns in the present appeals are concerned, there will be equality in the matter of competition. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and Dearness allowance together as it should have done, for the purpose of finding out whether the total pay packet in the appellants ' concerns can bear comparison with the total wage packet of comparable concerns; (ii) that there was no question of want of financial capacity and that Greaves Cotton & Co. which was the main company concerned in these appeals has a high standing in that region, and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowances for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff, it will be open to the Tribunal to fix the same rate of dearness Allowance for factory workmen; but in doing so the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total wages packet including basic wages fixed by it as well as dearness allowance (i.e. basic wage and dearness dearness allowance) and then compare it with the actual wage packet in other comparable concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen. HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the wages for these categories in comparable industries are, though it appears that some exemplars were filed before it; but the way in which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter shows that it paid scant regard to the exemplars filed before them and did not care to make the comparison for factory workers in the same way in Which it had made comparison for clerical and other subordinate staff. [375 G H] (2) The dearness allowance fixed by the Tribunal taking into account what was already prevalent in these concerns and also taking into consideration the trend in that area, can be successfully challenged so faras retrospective effect and adjustments as also fixation of wages & dearness allowance with respect to clerical and supervisory staff are concerned. [376 E F] (3) The principle therefore which emerges from these two decisions is that in applying industry cum Region formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there are a large number of concerns in that particular region carrying on the similar industry; in such a case in order that production cost may not be unequal and there may be equal competition, wages should generally be fixed on the basis of the comparable industries though more than the lowest, it cannot be said that the total income packet fixed is abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total Wage packet in another comparable concerns as to call for any interference with adjustments.

The appellants filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances. The trial Court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court having refused to grant leave to appeal to this Court, the mortgagees defendants 1 to 4 applied to and obtained from this Court special leave to Appeal against the decision of the Division Bench in so far as it upheld the rejection of their claims to Annappa 's half share in the mortgage property. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (i) The Rajinma had acted as karta was nowhere made by the defendants appellants in their written statement and, therefore, operated to extinguish the equity of redemption not only of Shiddana but also of Annaappa for there is sufficient evidence on record that a notice of relinquishment given by the registered occupant must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the 701 registered occupant, or that the registered proprietor has the right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in the occupancy. [775 D E] (ii) It is true that where there are more occupants than one, the notice of relinquished on behalf Of any occupant must be given by registered occupant; and the person, if any, in whose favour an occupancy is relinquished, or, if such 700 occupancy is relinquishment in favour of more persons than one. the principal of such persons, must enter into a written agreement to become the registered owner, and his name shall thereupon be substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant. That does not mean, in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof, that a Notice of relinquishment made by a registered occupant should necessarily be notice on the behalf of All occupants or some particular occupant, other than, the 701 Registered occupant, and that the unregistered occupant has the rights to give notice without referring to the others so as not to effect his interest in occupancy. The concluding paragraph of the section clearly recognises that a relinquishment may be in favour Of more persons only than one; the notice must necessarily mean a notice upon behalf of any occupant or any other particular occupant or that he has the power to give a notice with reference to all occupants so that to effect its interest in such occupancy. That do not mean , in the instant case, by reason only of his being the registered tenant, the Raj inama filed by him operated upon the entire occupancy and amounted to a relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers Shiddhappa and Annaiah for there was sufficient evidence that a notices of relinquishment were given by an unregistered occupant. The conclusion of the High Court that theRajinama and the Kabuliyat taken together evidenced a transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees and, thus operated to extinguishing the equity in redemption not merely of Shudana but of Anappa, for there has been sufficient evidence to show that a valid relinquishment was given by a Registered occupant.

The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at the Sugar Mill at Amroha at a time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Bulandshahr. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents I to 4 from service on the ground that 117 920 they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thus they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. " The appellant Mills filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Mill that (1) the right to transfer an employee by an employer from one of his concerns to another is implicit in every contract of service; and (2) there is no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant has the right, to transfer them to any of its concerns in any place and the question that arose was whether in the circumstances of each case the transfer from one concern to another was valid or amounted to victimization. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) It is not an express term of the contract of employment between the parties either express or implied that the employer has the inherent right to transferred his employee to another place where the business of the employer in the same line was situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract. [922 B] (b) The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant had the right under the contract to transfer respondents I and 4 to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment. It is well within the powers of the Labour Appellate Tribunal to entertain the appeal if it has the power to set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950.
