The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. On the clear finding in this case, this is not the position. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the ordinary worker and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. " Aggrieved by dismissal of the writ petition, the petitioners have filed this petition for special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution. In response to notice of this petition, a counter affi davit has been filed on behalf of respondent No. 2 reiterat ing the stand taken before the High Court. It has been stated therein that there is no vacancy in the establishment to absorb the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. The respondents are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb them immediately as regular workmen. On these facts, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. Petitioners claim regularisation of the services claiming that they were discharging the identical duties as regular workers and that for quite some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of their being no work available for them. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the peti tioners have been continuing on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is a work for them; and as such, there isno question of regularising the petitioners ' and giving him the pay o f regular workers whenever in fact he was not doing anything for a period of long time. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle Of regularisation of an daily rated employee and payment "to him" of the Pay equal to the that of regular workman arise only when a daily wager is doing his same work, as the normal worker and the there being no vacancy available in the Establishment for absorption of the petitioners. On this clear finding, this was not the situation. This petition must, therefore, fail. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf o respondent No 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the heating before us, we direct that all the 63 daily rated workers including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure R VI to the counter Affidavit be given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent No, 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. Subject to this direction, the special leave petition is dismissed. No costs. P.S. Petition dismissed. Summary: The petitioners claim that they being surplus to the requirement of the Project, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian ground so far. On behalf of Respondent No. 1 it has been contended that a Voluntary Retirement scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated employees has been framed, which is Annexure R IV to the Counter affi cation. This document shows the amount of retrenchment com pensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 Daily rated workmen under this Scheme. The 54 petitioners are included therein.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 173(4) and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court acquitted all the accused. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of section 173(3) had not been complied with, and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions Of sections 173, 207A and other sections of the Indian Penal Code have not been followed; and (ii) the omission was not sufficient to 37 vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence. HELD : (1) The provisions of sections 173 and 207 A(3), as amended by Act 26 of 1955, in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enjoining upon police officers concerned and magistrates before whom such proceedings are brought, to 293 see that all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. The word "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 207A is not mandatory but only directory because an omission by a police officer, to fully comply with the provisions contained in section 173, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. The words "shall", occurring both both in subsection (4), and in sub sections (3) and (3), which are material portions of that section, are in these terms : " (2) After forwarding a report under this section, the officer in charge of the police station shall, before the commencement of the inquiry or trial, furnish or cause to be furnished to the accused, free of cost, a copy of the report forwarded under sub section(1) and of all other documents or relevant extracts thereof on which the prosecution proposes to rely, including the statements and confessions, if any recorded under section 164 and the statements recorded under sub sections.(3) of Section 161 of all the persons whom the prosecution intends to examine as its witnesses. " The word 'shall ' occurring both by in sub cl. (4). is not directory but only mandatory, because an omissions by a Police officer, or to fully complied with the provision of section 172, should be allowed not to have any such far reaching effects as to rendering the proceedingsincluding the trial at the court Of Session wholly incompetent. [293 G H; 293 A B] (2)(a) The omission on the part of the Police Officer concerned or of the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, has caused prejudice to the appellant in the interest of justice, and the irregularity is curable by reference to section 537 of the Criminal Procedure Code as no case of prejudice has been made out. [294 G H] (b) The word `shall ' occurs both in cl. 4(4)(a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f), (g), and (h). It is not necessary that before the Magistrate who was holding his inquiries under section 207 A, any grievance was made that the provision had not not been comply with by the police officer concerned or the magistrate at whom such committal proceedings were brought to see that the accused has not been furnished with such documents or any of them, he should cause the same to be so furnished. But it is only after the conviction and sentences of the accused persons, that the Magistrate can proceed further in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Code.

The respondent Municipality issued a notice to the appellant under section 153A of the Act requiring him to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government and as mentioned in the notice so that rendering saline or corrupting the water of wells, tanks, ponds or other water receptacles, or prejudicially affecting the fertility of the ,oil in the surrounding areas may be stopped. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of section 153 A on the ground that it violated articles 19(1)(C) and (2) of the constitution. Held, that the provisions of sections 153A and 153A do not offend article 19(i)(C). It is plain that before the appellant could be called upon to comply with the requisition of the respondent Municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special Officer ought to have decide and report whether a nuisance exists or not. If the existence of a nuisance was assumed because that was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report only as to the manner in which the effluent should be discharged. It is open to the person to whom the notice has been issued to accept the assertion of the municipality that the nuisance in question exists and to agree to comply therewith, the Municipality may appoint a special judicial officer " to hold an inquiry into the matter. The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfied of the Municipalities as to existence of such a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned.

The Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 was enacted to provide for punishment of persons in unlawful possession of railway stores who cannot satisfactorily account how they came by the same. By section 2 "railway stores" are defined to mean any article (a) which is the property of any railway administration and (b) which has been used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. It reads: "If any person is found, or is proved to have been in possession of any article of railway Stores reasonably suspected of being stolen or unlawfully obtained, and cannot account satisfactorily how he came by, the same, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, orwith both. " The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Railway Stores Act, 1954 on the ground that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this 189 kind were usually sold or that he has bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the same and that railway articles were mixed with other goods in the bags. The trial court convicted him under section 4 of the Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The prosecution must prove that the articles belonged to any particular railway administration but which has not been discarded or rejected for further use would be outside the definition of railway store stores. In most cases the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to the effect that the goods belonged to a particular Railway administration but they were used or were intended to been used for the construction or operation of a Railway. In the case of goods which had not been put to use evidence would have to he led to establish that they had been manufactured for such us,. 191 The evidence 'in the case before the courts did not establish that the items mentioned in his report were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the , Act and as such the question of punishment under section 5 did not arise.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondents on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means (a) The person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and (b) In the event of death of such person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily residing and in the Case of premises let out for residential or business purpose, ordinarily carrying on business with him in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The suit was decreed by the Courts below. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the courts below and decreeing the suit for eviction of the appellants from the demised shop in Jaipur. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of this case. But the appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised property governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to t he rights in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1) (a). The heirs of the tenants of commercial premises are entitled to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Rent Acts, an irrepara ble mischief which the Legislature would never have intended was likely to be caused. [9A B] 1.2 In view of the termination of the contractual tenancy, the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs of such tenants become entitled to inherit the status and position of the statutory tenant on his death, the LegislatUre which has created this right has thought it fit in the ease of residential premises to limit the rights of the heirs in the manner and to the extent provided in Section 13(i)(a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act. [10B C] 1:3 In the instant case, despite the termination o f the contractual lease, the tenant continued to remain in possession as on the date of the suit as statutory tenants. The succession having been opened to the appellants and succeeded in September 1966 to the estate of the deceased tenant without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable Interest in the Lease hold right held by the tenant Smt. Anandi, the Amendment Acts being admittedly prospective in operation, does not have the effect of divesting their vested rights in the leased premises governed by Section 13 (1)(a). [10E F] 1 :4 The Amending act does not bring about any change in the status or legal position of a contractual tenant unless there are contrary provisions in the Act; but the appellants succeed to the inherited inter est in the licence hold right of a demised premises held by Smt. They continued to be in possession even after determination of the contract as statutory tenant, without any riatus or restriction on his heritable interest. Therefore, despite termination of contractual tenancy the tenancy right are heritable, and the heir of such tenant is entitled to enjoying the protection of the Rent Act.

The appellant Board is willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Funds Act, 1952. The employees also contended that the services of the workmen of a Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under section 64 and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The Industrial Tribunal accepted this contention and held that all employees of the appellant Board should not have the benefit of the Contributory Provident Funds Scheme to all workmen other than those who were covered by it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant Board that the State Government is the financier of the respondent Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum, and therefore there could be no difference between the Boards ' Contributory Provident fund scheme and the Scheme under the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The financial capacity of the employer is to be taken into consideration while deciding matters regarding benefits to be made available to its employees. Payment towards provident fund and gratuity is expense to be met by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of Provident Fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden Of wage structure in the interest of social justice. Even so it was noticed that the stability of the industry as well as the fact that the onus of provident fund & gratuity did not result, in some reduction in profits; but if the industry is in a stable condition and the burden is of Provident fund and Gratuity does not results in loss of the employers that burden would have to been borne by it like the cost of wage structure In the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the board, it should. be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [63 E F] (2) The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the gratuity reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence absence of detailed examination, of the financial status of the employee. [64 C D] (3) The Board makes subventions to the Board for the purposes of the act. Under section 67 after meeting its operating maintenance and management expenses and after provision has been made for the payment of taxes on its income and profits the revenues of the State have tobe distributed as far as they are available in the following order, namely: (i) interest on bonds not guaranteed under section 66; (ii) the balance to be appropriated to a fund to be called the Development Fund to be utilised for (a) purposes beneficial, in the opinion of the Boards, to electrical development in the State; and (b) repayment of loans advanced to the board under section64 and required to be repaid: 47 Provided that where no such loan is outstanding, one half of the balance remaining aforesaid shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of the state.

The respondent wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for grant of maintenance. The Magistrate dismissed the application on the ground that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of the maintenance. In revision before the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse live with the husband merely because her husband was impotable and unable to discharge his marital obligation, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a valid ground within the meaning of the second proviso so as to make the refusal of the wife 's refusal to live With her husband fully justified and entitled to maintenance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decisions referred to above in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Babu Lal Dixit, J sounded a very pragmatic note on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointed out that where a husband contracts a marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress this would be deemed to be a " just ground" within the ambit of the first proviso so that to make an order of maintenance if he was satisfied that there was just ground, for doing so. If this is so, can it be said that the ground of impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the civil law to be in a good ground not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. But that is a very different thing from holding that no evidence of cruelty can be admitted in a proceeding under the section to prove, not indeed cruelty as a ground for separate maintenance, but also the conduct and acts of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife. [707 B C] 2.1 In the instant case, it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impotsuable and is unable to discharging his marital obligations, this will amount to either both legal & mental cruelty as contemplated by the aforesaid proviso for the respondent wife ' s refusal to living with her would be entitled to maintain from her husband according to his means. In view of our decision in this case it follows that the decisions referred t o above in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [807 D E] 2:2 The decisions relied on by the learned Judge of the High Courts are hereby set aside and the order taking a similar view must, accordingly, be held not to be good law.

The plaintiff was the owner of a portion of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. He had also prayed for damages for wrongful occupation in respect of a part of the property and rent for another portion, for the period from 1st January, 1964 till possession of the land is delivered to the plaintiff. The defendants were the Union of India and the State of Gujarat. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that by virtue of these orders the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had come to be vested in the Municipality, there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land in question, that its right over the property was never recognised by the Union Government or the State Government and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show, that as early as July, 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of the plaintiff had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the Union India and that possession was handed over by the Government of India to the State Govt. on 7th July, 1952 for use. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 vested in it only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the municipality. In this while referring to the suit lands which were stated to be in their possession a remark has been made to the effect: "The Bhavnagar Municipality claims the land on the basis that the whole assets of the Bhavnagar town planning Department had been transferred to them by the orders of his Highness, Bhavnagar, State in 1948 and they are collecting the Revenue from the farmers. As seen earlier, possession was with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to the land was not vested in them. The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Government and was performing the duty of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was thus performing a public duty. He was attached to the office of the Superintendent of the Salt Department and was attached thereto to the Office of the Assistant Salt Officer. The appellant was, therefore, an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code and being such public servant he could not be convicted of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. Held, that an "officer in the Service or pay" of Government performing as such a public function entrusted to him by the Government was one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. The true test, therefore in order to determine whether a person is an officer of the government, is: (1) whether he is entrusted with the performance or discharge of any public duty; and (2) whether it is performing duties immediately ' auxiliary to those of some one who was an Officer of the State within the terms of section21(9), Indian Penal code. The question for consideration before the learned Judges of the Lahore High Court was whether a Quarter Master 's clerk as such was just a Babu and no more an officer than a labourer or menial employed and paid by Government to do public work (See Queen vs Nachimuttu, Ahad Shah vs Emperor, ; , referred to.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C for recovery of revenue due to him under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 (hereinafter referred to as "the said Act"). The auction was notified for June 14,1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the said auction sale the Respondent filed 847 an appeal in the court of Sub judge, 1 st Class Patiala C. in respect of which they had to pay a sum of Rs. Ultimately, recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. The Collector dismissed the suit so far as it related to the portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent injunction with regard to the portions in which liquor shop is situated. The Respondent then filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala, being Regular Second Appeal No. 2944 of 1980 before the High Court. The Single Judge allowed the said second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, inserted in the said section 60 by a State amendment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect Of, the Respondent 's half share in the aforesaid property were not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery or recovery of Revenue due to the State. There is no provision in the Punjab Act which makes the provisions of section 60 applicable to attachment and sales under any of her statutes made expressly applicable thereto. The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the aforesaid Act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said Acts. [848G H; 849A B] 2. Section 60 does not apply to an attachment and Sale under any other statute made expressly or applicable thereto.. The attachment was levied under the provisions Of the Punjab Excise Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provision of the aforesaid Acts. The property, if My, which is exempt from seizure and sale, in revenue Recovery proceedings under this Act would also be only those properties as were so exempted under the Act.

The lands in question were acquired by the Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that such right to compensation had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as at the date of the death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law P inasmuch as the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in the original assessment had been valued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court, and the High court 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on wrong basis was liable to be set aside. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent having merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore, the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of those lands on the date when the original assessments were made. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that assigning that the right to receive compensation survived and it was that right which was being prosecuted by the heirs of Rashid in Civil Court the impugned notice had been issued under s.61 with a view to get over the bar of limitation under s 73A, which would otherwise be applicable to a notice under s 59(a) of the Act and (b) that for purposes of section 61 the land acquisition proceedings and Land References in the Civil Courts could not be regarded as part of the assessment record and he so called mistake discovered by reference to such other record was not a mistake apparent from the record and as such the impugned notices were liable to quashed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the res respondent had merely accepted his value of lands as assessed by the Land References and, consequently, the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of 'the estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings. [330F] 1.2 In the first place the said property, namely, the increased compensation was not in existence 1. at the time of the original Assessment under section 73A of the Land Acquiring Act, which was on the basis of compensation awarded to the Special Assistant Collector as the proper valuation he must be deemed to have adopted that evaluation as his own estimate of the lands which he wanted to enhance by relying upon the valuation made by another authority, namely the City Civil Court. [331F] 2.1 In the second place the respondent must resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date on which the original assessments were made, but what we find is that the said notice was issued by the respondent on the wrong assumption that the acquired land still formed part of ' state of the deceased which passed on his death, that the valuation for those lands adopted on the previous occasion which was On the basis Of compensation awarded in the Land Reference and, thus, such property had escaped assessment to tax. [431G] 2:2 The High Courts have attempted to distinguished the above decisions by stating as well as the contents of the communication sent by the Respondent to the appellants representative on January 9, 1970 clearly suggest that the impugned notification was issued under section61 with an intention to get about the bar for limitation under section73A, and that for purpose of Section 61 the Land acquisition proceedings, and Land Reference in the civil Court could not have been regarded as a part of assessment record.

The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986, and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors as per the provisions of section 73FF, and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 1167 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The notice further said: "Because you have remained in arrars of the loan instalments as referred above to the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank, under Section 73FF(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act, 1960 a person committing defaults ceased to be the Executive Committee (member) or Director. " The appellant 's revision petition against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Cooperative Societies, Nagpur on 15.2,.1988 holding inter alia, that section 73F of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21.10.86 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21. 10.1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The appellant filed an appeal against this order before the Divisional Deputy Registrar, who dismissed the same holding that section 78FF became applicable from 6.8.'86 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.1986 i.e. the date when he was declared elected as Director; and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21 10. 1986 when he became elected as director, he was still not a defaulter in presenti on the date of notice and the provisions contained in section 78 were not attracted; and (iii) that even assuming that the appellant had repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 73B(1), on 31.3.1986, on 18 8.86, when he had been elected as Directors, he became defaulter under section 74FF(2) of Act, and rejected the appellant ' s contention that section73FF became attracted from 6 8. 1986 as per Govt. Notification issued in June 1986 i. e., the date on which he was deemed to be vacant; (iv) that as the appellant having repaid the loan before he impugned notice was issued, he could not have acted under section 79(1); and (v) that the provisions relating to setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellants having continued to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loans before the notice was given would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section78.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from services. The State Government preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [34G H] (2)(a) It further provides that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note I to Rule 33 of the said Bombay Civil Service Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules. This rule further provides for withholding or withdrawing a pension or any part thereof if the pensioner is convicted of grave misconduct either during or after the completion of his service provided that before no order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note 1 to Rule 34 of the Rules shall be followed. [35A B] (b) The reduction of pension by 50% was too harsh and disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent. In his report to the State government the Collector of Kolhapur held that the respondent 's action was helpful to Shri Khatavane to sell the sugar in the black market, and it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government Servant. He recommended that since the respondent had already superannuated from service a lenient view should be taken and reduction in pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made. The High Court committed serious error in holding that the Government had no power to initiate any proceedings against him after he had retired from Service on attaining his age of retirement, and instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension. [36F G] (c) The State of Maharashtra has preferred this Appeal against the judgment of the High court dated February 13, 1987 and directed the State to reconsider the question of reduction of respondent ''s pension by 25 per cent in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the rules. [37G H; 38A B C] (d) The Government had power to reduce the amount payable to respondent but having regard to the facts and circumstances, of the case, we are of the opinion that the reduction of Pension by 50 percent was too severe and disproportionate and to the misconduct proved against him.

Section 3(4) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 provides that a landlord can evict his tenant if he satisfies two conditions. The first condition is that before a District Magistrate grants permission to the landlord to sue his tenant, he shall issue notice to the tenant and give him an opportunity to represent his case before the application of the landlord is dealt with on merits; and in such a case, the failure of the District Magistrate to comply with the mandatory provision% prescribed in that behalf would render the order passed by him completely invalid and a plea that an order has been passed by the District Collector without complying with the provisions of section 3(3) of Act would be open for examination before a civil court. Held, that the High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional ,visional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 k 3) is invalid in law; and so, he came to the conclusion that the appellants ' suit was incompetent. Section 3(5) of U. P. ( Temporary) Control Of Rent and eviction Act, 1948 provides that the order of the Commissioner under sub section (3) shall subject to any order passed under section 7 F, be final. If it is shown by a party impeaching the validity of the order in a civil suit that the Collector has acted illegally or with material irregularity or has wrongly refused to act, he can make an appropriate order; and the order thus made by him is final under sub s (4), subject to such orders that the State Government may pass under section 3 F.

Article 317(1) of the Constitution provides that, subject to the provisions of clause (3), the Chairman or any other person of a Public Service Commission shall only be removed from his office by order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court, on reference being made to it by the President. The power of the Chairman to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(2) is not subject to any condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That article provides that the Chairman and every other member of a public Service Commission can only be remove from his Office on the grounds of misbehaviour, after the Apex Court has on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 642(1), reported that the chairman or such other member, as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removed. In exercise of the power conferred by Article 317 (1) the President has referred for consideration of this Court the question "as to whether the facts found upon by an independent fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. The inquiry which this Court is required to hold is not into the limited question whether, on the basis of facts found by the president, the charge of assault is made out and whether the misconduct is of such a nature as to require his removal from the office of the Member of the Public Service commission. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 317 provides that subject to clause (1), theChairman or any member of the public service Commission can be removed by the order of a President on any ground other than with the leave of this court. In case it is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar of the Supreme court for extension of time. The evidence to be recorded by the learned judge will be limited to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits before him within the constraints of the following guidelines: (1)(a) The affidavits filed in this Court will be treated as the examination in chief of the respective witnesses; and (b) Witnesses who have not filed affidavits in this court may be summoned or requested by the counsel for the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial. It is an idle complaint that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by his learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. The recording of evidence will be over by September 30, 1983. In other words, no person who has not filed an affidavit in this case will be examined or cross examined as a witness except with the permission of this Hon'ble Court. [615C D] 2. Article 318 provides that "subject to the provision of clause(3), (i) the Chairman, or any officer of a State Public Service Commissions shall only have the powers to remove from office his office on the view of misbehaviour and if he is allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter." [616D] 3. Article 320 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in clause (2), the President may by order remove from the Office of a member of Public Service any person who had not filed any affidavit except with leave of the Court, and (ii) the order or removal can be passed after the expiry of the period specified in clauses (1).

The appellant plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. Chatterjee, has submitted that the approach made by the High Court was wholly incorrect and it had misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowment was a private one and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant plaintiffs that (i) the approach taken by the trial court was wholly erroneous and it has misconstrued the documents and documents filed in the suit to show the private nature of the endowment; (ii) there was no evidence or document produced in support of the plea that there was any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members of the public nor was there any averment in the deed to show, if the management of the property dedicated was in the hands of the strangers or members of their family. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question as to whether an endowment is of a private nature or of a public character has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application; (2) Where, however, a document is available to prove the nature and origin of the dedication and the recitals of the document show that a control and management of a temple is retained with the founder or his descendants, and that extensive properties are dedicated for the purpose of the maintenance of the temple belonging to the founder himself, this will be a conclusive proof to show whether the endowment had been made by a person who has no issue and who after installing the deity entrusts the management to members of his family; (3) Where the origin of an endowment cannot be ascertained, the question whether the user of the Temple by members or the Government was as of right that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the dedication was of a Public nature. [833H; 834A B] (4) The mere fact that members of a community used to come to the temple with out any hindrance also does not necessarily mean that the temple is a public temple, for members of such family or their descendants do attend private temples. It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed therein in a temple, the worship of the deity is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the idol, and therefore, the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of endowment. Some of the extracts of this document which are undisputed, in our opinion, clearly and conclusively show that it was of private nature and the intention of the founder was merely to instal a family idol in the Temple.

The appellant Bank formerly known as Bharat Bank Ltd., agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out the terms of the said arrangement more effectively and to secure the interest of the attorneys are desirous of appointing the Bharat Bank Limited, as our lawful attorneys in all matters relating to the receipt of all payments under the contract made or to be made hereafter and also to take steps in his name and on his behalf. On December 12, 1952, the appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that TakhatMal had no right to attach it. The Trial Court held that the power of attorney dated July 13, 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies due under the bills in favour of the appellant. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court reversed the decree and decreed the suit. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Bank that the Power of attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the Attorneys have agreed to advance moneys against supply bills for payments to be received by us under the said contracts more effectively, and to obtain cheques for sums payable to him under the agreements directly in their own name or in payment of such bills or other amounts and to cash and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards and in repayment of the advances made orto be made hereinafter and all monies due from us to the attorney 's in any account whatever soever". HELD: The power of Attorney coupled with a endorsement on it, created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment in favour by Malhotra to pay the appellant bank out of the moneys receivable under the bill and amounted to a equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. In Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur (2) this Court held, that there was an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific Fund coming to the debtor or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order directing such person to pay such funds to the creditor will create a valid equitable charge upon such fund, in other words, wfll operate as an equitable Assignment of the debts or fund to which the order refers refer. The power Of attorney coupled with its endorsement on a bill dated 7 9 1948 created an Interest in a particular specific fund, and was a clear engagement by Malhotrato pay the appellants out of their assets in their hands the costs of this appeal as also the costs in the courts below.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said Company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But on further appeal to the tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In this appeal by certificate it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the receipts in question were not salary and the same having not been assessed as his salary, the assessment order relating to that item of receipt was not legal. Held: (i) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ representing the interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund or any interest on such contributions cannot be said to be either interest on securities; income from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered as "income from other source" and brought to tax under section 56. Section 56(I) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under the head income "from other sources" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. The receipt by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from the purview of that expression any payments received by him from a provident fund, his own contributions to the Fund or anyinterest on such contribution. From that it follows that the receiving of Rs 27,949/ by the appellant in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered "income" and bring to tax Under section 56(1)(iv). Hence there is no need to call into aid any of these rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. The respondent was not represented before this Court.
