In the State of West Bengal and Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc., , this Court held that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. "Specified industry" is defined in the Act as meaning any industry specified in Schedule I. The cess was payable by all persons carrying on a specified industry, and every Local Authority and is computed on the principle of water consumption by such persons or local authorities as the circumstances of each case may require. " On behalf of the State it was contended that the word 'vegetable ' in Item (6) of Schedule I to the Cess Act must be construed as understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense meaning 'that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it and so construed, it denotes those classes of vegetables which are grown in a kitchen garden or in a farm and are used for the table. " Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'sewage ' in the context does not attract the botanic meaning. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within the meaning of 'pro cessing vegetable product ' in Entry 15 of Schedule 1 of the Cess Rules. [515G H] 2.1 In order to bring an industry within any of these entires in Schedule 1 it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. If the bottanic definition of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule II like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry 14. [615C D] 2:2 The word "vegetables" has been used in entry 15 on the ground that it is based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it This Court in State of Bihar & Ors. ; , with reference to the meaning to be ascribed for such words shall normally depend on the nature, scope and purpose of the statute in which it is occurring and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. In the context in which the word "sewage" is used in Entry 14 it does not bring within the botsanic colour. The Sugar manufacturing industry does not, however, come under Entry 15 on Schedule I of the cess Act. [525E F] 2(a) It has to also be borne in mind that this Act with which we are concerned is an Act imposing li ability for cess. P. In Union of India vs Delhi Cloth and General Mills, AIR 1963 SC 79 this Court pointed out: "The word 'vesgetable product ' means product of or made of or out of vegetable. 'Vegetables as understood by common parlance are not products of manufacture unless we say that agriculture is an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry." [525A B] 2.(b) The sugar industry manufacturing sugar itself is not an industry under the meaning Of Entry 15 and a fortio ri the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry as contemplated in Item 15. [500C D].

Section 10(3) (a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 provides for the determination of fair rent of a building on the application of the tenant or landlord. Section 10(1) provides that the grounds are default of payment of rent, sub letting of premises used for a purpose other than that for which it was leased, commission of acts of waste, conduct amounting to nuisance to the occupiers of the other portions in the same building, securing of alternative accommodation by the tenant and denial of the title of the landlord. The respondent filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10 (3) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of him on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ' and that in the context of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context in which it occurs, the word may have been used cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in Section 10. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression business ' occurring in section 10( 3)(a) (iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice o profession like that of an advocate or a Doctor which had nothing commercial about it was not 'business within the ambit of Section 5(3)(a). In Stuchbery & Ors. vs General Accident Fire and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd., , this very question whether the practice was a 'business' within the definition of that expression in section 2(g) (ii) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease Rent and eviction) Control act, 1960, the same meaning that the word might have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. The word must be interpreted in the light of the statute in which the statute occurs and not in the sense of other statutory enactments or in any manner alien thereto. [14C D] 2. Section 4 provides for determination of a fair rent and section 10 (1) which bars the eviction from a non residential building where "the landlord is not occupying a nonresidential building in a city town or village concerned which is his own or to the possession of which he is entitled whether under the Act or otherwise (a) for the purposes of a business which in the opinion of the Controller, the landlord bona fide proposes to commence". [15E F] 3. The words 'business " occurring in Section 2(h)(i) are used in wide sense and so as not to include any profession. [16F G] 4. In Stodbery & Anr. vsGeneral Accident Fire & Life Assurance Corpn Ltd., ; , referred to.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which the appellants were the partners on the condition that interest would be payable @ 7/9 per cent per month and that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The respondent accepted the said proposal and thereafter a letter dated 29 September 1942 was written by Ram Ratan Gupta to the respondent recording the agreement that "a sum of Rupees 4,50,000 was deposited in the name of M/S India Supplies whereupon the appellant would place to the credit of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills a sum Rs. 2,00.000 with the appellant in the deposit account. The letter further shows that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners and the Gupta group on behalf of India Supplies on the one hand and that all that happened was that in place of Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills the respondent became the creditor of the Firm of the appellants. On the question whether it was a case where money was deposited under an agreement and that it was payable on demand or whether it Was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs 4, 00,000 by the respondent with the respondent under an Agreement that the same would be paid on 577 demand. Held, that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the amount deposited. It is also important to bear in mind that a demand in the year 1943 for a part of the money would not be effective because there were common partners in the firms of the respondent and the appellant. There must be a unqualified demand of the whole amount before the Limitation can star In case of demands for return, the limitation could star in cases of demand and return of that amount. It was not a case for the respondent giving loan to the appellant for the obvious reason that the history of the transactions between the appellant and Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills show.% that the appellant had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use of the sum. One of the terms in the award was that the award in respect of Lakshmi Rantan Cotton Mills and India Supplies would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him only to the one point and it was clearly stated by the senior counsel that he had a strong almost unanswerable case on merits but he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arose squarely in this case. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of Mr. Jethmalani who was aware of the proceedings in the Court and did not dispute the fact that he was already in custody when the order of detention came to be served and since the detenu was already under custody, the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for put ting him back in jail. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining Authority in making an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authori ty was aware about the fact whether the detenu had confined his arguments to one point settled the writ petition as senior counsel with the allegations quoted above in paragraph 2 of the writ peti tion, but where the offences in respect of which the detenu has been accused are so interlinked and continuous in character and are of such nature that these affect continuous mainte nance of essential supplies and thereby jeo pardise the security of the State, then sub ject to other conditions being fulfilled, a man being in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply. [849E F] 2. The facts of the present case clearly show that the petitioner was in custody at the most one day. Charge sheet had not been submitted against him in the criminal case and he had been remanded to the judicial custody on the 27th of February, 1986 with the direction to be produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th of Feb., 1986. The Court also indicated that it was not a matter of jurisdition but had to be decided on the facts of each case. Therein it was said: "In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu having been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, the bail application had to he opposed and in case bail was granted, challenge against that order in the higher forum had tobe raised. Where a person accused of certain offences whereunder he is undergoing trial or has been acquitted, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention but the relevant facts in connection with the making of the order may differ and that may make a difference in the application of the principle that a detention order can be passed against a man while he is in detention or in jail; but where offences in regard to which the petitioner is accused are such interlinked, and continuous, in character, and are such nature, that these affects continuous mainie nanceof essential supplies, thereby jib pardisethe security of State,, then subsection (1) does not preclude the authority from passing an order against a detenu whilst he is already in detention and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that the order Of detention became necessary.

The petitioners, who were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department, filed writ petitions before the High Court contending that even though 602 many of them have been working for the last ten years as casual A labourers, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not being regularly employed, they were not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: (1) The petitioners are directed to prepare a scheme on a rational basis for absorbing as far as possible the casual semi skilled/skilled labour working in the Telecom. Wing of P & T Department will be as under: (i) Casual semi skilled /skilled labourers who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more; and (ii) Casual Semi skilled/Skilled workers who strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 270 and Rs.260 350 as the case may be, and that there should not be any variation in the respective job con tent. [630C D] (2) The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to casual semikilled/s skilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period Of more than six months. These enhanced rates of Daily Wages are applicable to the semi skilled and unskilled/s semi skilled labourers who strictly comply with the job contents of corresponding posts in scale of Rs 210 270 andRs.260350 as the cases may be and that they should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labourer or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourers for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraph Department. [600E F] (3) The benefits of increased rate of daily wage will not, however, be admissible in the cases of those who had completed 720/1200 days in 3/5 years, where the continuous spell of duty is intervened by an period of more than 6 months. This enhanced rates will be without prejudice to absorption of casual semi-skilled/S skilled labour against regular vacancies as and when they occur.

The assessee was assessed under section 66A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. He filed a return showing an income below the taxable limit as required by section 34(1)(a) of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not issue a notice under section 34 after a return was already made before it and the benefit of the extended period of limitation for assessment available under the first proviso to sub section (3) of section 34 of one year from the service of the notice under sub section(1) of that section was not available in this case. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the contention of the assessee and gave its opinion that the Department ought to have issued a notice within the assessment year, and if no return was made within the time fixed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a "best judgment" assessment. The High Court held that since he had submitted a return under section 22(3) on January 5, 1950, the assessment, if any, had to be completed before March 31, 1950 as required in section 34 (1)(b) of Act and subs. 120 Section 22 of the Income tax Officer had reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of an assessee to make a return of his income under section 24(2), for any year, he could not possibly be 'treated as a return filed under section24(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that since the return filed on January 4, 1950 was a return which showed no assessable income, there was no scope for the issuance of a notice unders. 22(2); (ii) that even a return made in response to a notice issued under section 27(1), if filed belatedly under section 25(3), could not be treated as such a return submitted under section 26(1); and (iii) that there was, therefore, no scope of the issuance Of a notice thereunder unders. 23(2). HELD : (i)(a)(b)(c)(d)(e)(f) of Income tax Rules, 1922, does not mean that even if a return has been filed in response thereto under section 19(3); it is still a good return for all purposes under the Act, so as to bring the matter within section 34.(1)(c) of Indian Income Tax Act. [857 D] (b) The notice under s. 22 (2) was served on the assessee on January 2, 1950 and a return in answer to that notice could be filed under s 24(1.) before assessment, and for this there is no limit of time prescribed by section 24 (3). [858 E F] (c) It would appear from this that if the return has not been filed within the period allowed by or under sub s. (1) or sub s.(2), or having furnished a return, under either of those sub sections, discovers any omission or wrong statement therein, he may furnish a return or a revised return as the case may be at any time before the assessment is made.

Section 9 of the , insofar as it is material, is to empower the Central Government to make a scheme for the constitution of the Board of Directors so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. Sub clause (c) of Clause 3 provides that every Board of Director of a correspond ing new bank constituted under any scheme made under subsection (1), shall include (a) representative of the employee, and of depositors, of such bank, and (b) such other persons as may represent the interests of each of the following categories, namely, farmers, workers and artisans, to be elected or nominated in such manner as may be specified in the scheme. Section 9 provides that the Central Govern ment shall, by notification in the official Gazette constitute a Board of directors so as, to include representative of employees and others speci tied to it by the representative Union. Such appointment, though made out of, and restricted to, the panel furnished by the Union, is in effect a nomination of the one preferred by the Central Gover nment. Section 10 provides for constitution of Board of Management so asto include representatives o f the employees of the nationalised bank, within a date to be specified by the central Government. Clause (c), inter alia, provides that if election were to be construed to be the appropriate mode of choosing the representatives of employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnish ed by the representatives Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. Clause 3(c) provides that each Board shall include representative o f such bank and (d) such others as may represented the interests o f each of its categories, viz., farmers, employees and artisan, to represent the interest of each such category, namely; agriculturists, workers, artisans and to be nominated in the manner chosen by it so as To appoint the true representatives of th e employees. Clause 4 provides that in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, the Central Gov ernment shall, after consultation with th e Reserve Bank, constitute the Board for a period of three years from amongst the employees specified on the panel submitted by the repre sentatives of the concerned employees fur nished to it under clause (b). Clause 5 provides that one Director, from among the employees referred to in clauses (a), (b)(i) and (c ) such other person as may represents the interests Of each of them, shall be appointed by the State Government after consultation wit th the Reserve bank. The Central Governmen t has also been empowered to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it is incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employee to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govt. to continue the: practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repres sentatives o f employees and, if necessary, to amend it suitably for that purpose. In the case of workmen employees, the Director is appointed by t he Central Government from out of a panel of three such persons fur ned to it.

The assessee, who was the respondent, was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1 lakh on an assessee during the pendency of an appeal before it. The assessee preferred appeals to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalty imposed. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Appellate Tribunal had no power under the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to stay recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power of granting stay as incidental or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction and that it is only at the earlier stage of appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the statute confers such a power on the Incometax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee but that can hardly be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220(6) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of the appeal before him. [69G H] The Appellate Assistant Commissioners and the Appellate Tribunals are given the power, under the Code of Civil Procedure when trying a suit in respect of the matters specified in the section. There can be no manner of doubt that by the provisions of sections 254 and 255 of the Act or the Income taxes Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate tribunal to stay proceedings relating to the recovery of tax, either in whole or in part on furnishing suitable security, is a matter for the legislature to consider. [70E F] The power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine manner or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power for doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was appointed as Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial. He was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with having committed offences punishable under sections 7 and 8 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The charge against him was that he had received bribes in the discharge of his duties. On November 17, 1952, he was placed under suspension and on August 18, 1953 he was found guilty of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good but that his transfer should, therefore, come after sometime and that in the meantime his work might be closely watched. On July 28, 1953, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that no case as required by the said sub paragraph was registered against the respondent in the police station. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the enquiry was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities; and (2) if the order was held to have been made under the statutory power conferred upon the Superintendent of Police, the regulations providing for investigation in the first place under chapter XIV of the Criminal Procedure Code were only directory in nature, and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect the validity of the order. HELD: (1)(a) The departmental trial was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial inquiry and therefore it fell within the express terms of para. 486 of the Indian Police Regulations. From the facts already narrated, the conduct of the respondent when he was officer incharge of the police Station, Intiath, was the subject matter of (1). Civil Appeal No. The Sub Divisional Magistrate made inquiry in respect of seven of the charges which were the subject matters of the criminal trial and; submitted a report to the Superintendent Of Police recommending the transfer of the Respondent and suggesting that in view of the said complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect, the validity or invalidity of the orders of dismissal; and the departmental enquiry was held at an earlier stage. In such cases, and in other cases until and unless a magisterial enquiry is ordered, inquiry will be made under order of the Superintendent in accordance with the following rules. Paragraph 489: "A police officer may be departmentally tried under section7 of the Act after he has been tried judicially; In this case, the departmental proceedings were held subsequent thereto to the completing of the Magisterial inquiry, and therefore, it fell outside the express term of para 486 of Indian Police Regulation. From these facts it would be hypertechnical to hold that there was no magisterial Inquiry in respect Of the matter which was the subjectmatter of the disciplinary trial. [666 C D] (b) The High Courts were right in holding that the respondent was charged with committing cognizable offences and, therefore sub paragraph (1), of para 489 governed the situation and that as no case, as required under the said Sub paragraph, was registered, the order dismissing was invalid.

The appellant was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of Dr. Sen and Dr. P. Sen who were junior to him. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that when a post in Ophthalmology Speciality at Willingdon Hospital was created on February 1, 1971, by conversion of one post from amongst unspecified specialists ' grade posts in supertime Grade II that post could only have been filled in by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists' grade, i.e. category 'C ' under 1963 Rules and the strength of Specialists ' grades was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 posts added to super time grade II is required to be filled in, it becomes an addition to the strength strength of that speciality and the filling in of such post shall be governed by rule 8 (3). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When a post from among unspecified Specialists' posts was converted into a specified post which means specified in the speciality in which a need has been felt from amongst them amongst those in the specialities ' grade belonging to that speciality, and in order of their inter se seniority a promotion could be given. In passing a contention of the appellant that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into an unspecified post it can only be filled by promotion yet when some one who is already in that grade is transferred to the newly created post and the post vacated by such transferred employee is offered by way of promotion which in fact was done in this case there was no violation of the rule. [8H; 8A] 2. When an unsspecified specialists " grade posts" were converted to a specified category in super time Grade II it becomes a addition to that strength of the speciality and filling in such post would be governed under rule 8(3). But if there is some substance, though there is none, in the contention on behalf of the appellants that whenever unspecifiedspecialists ' posts are converted into separate specialities and were filled in after amongst those who were qualified to be promoted in the respective speciality in whom the post was created he could be said to have been superseded in violation of article 16. If this contention were to prevail, apart from anything else, appellant himself would not have been qualified for promotion to super Time grade II in February 1971 because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists" grade officers formed on September 9, 1966. Therefore, if there was some substance or justification for giving a direction that the appellant should be considered for the post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion ofDr. Sen, it is difficult to entertain the contention that in refusal to accept promotion at Simla appellant was never superseded by any one junior to Dr. S.N. Sen. The matter must remain at that stage and there is no justification for granting a direction to the appellant to consider his case for the posts which are deemed to be fallen vacant on the invalidated of promotion. [9H; 10A] 3. When the need is felt and a post is converted from an uns specified post it cannot be filled up by promotion but when some other one who was already in the same grade is converted into the specified post, it can either be filled only by promotion or not some one else who is on top of the general seniority list in Specialists " grades or general duty officers ' grade from which promotion is to be made.

Section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 provides that if after the commencement of this Act any person acquires any land by inheritance or gift from a person to whom he is an heir, any person acquiring in any other manner any land and which with or without the lands already owned or held by him exceeds in the aggregate the permissible area, then he shall within the period prescribed, furnish to the Collector a return in the prescribed form and manner giving the particulars of all lands and selecting the land not exceeding in the total permissible area which he desires to retain, and if the land of such person is situated in more than one patwar circle, he shall also furnish a declaration required by section 5 A. The Collector ignoring the transfer of 167 bighas of land by respondent No. 1 safe ashore and so he sought harbourage by moving the High Court under article 226 where he urged that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B, of the Act. The State Government or any officer em powered by it in this behalf shall be competent to utilize any surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected, or to be ejected under clause (i) of sub section (1) or section 9. (a) Explanation. such utilization of any surplus land will not affect the right of the landowner to receive rent from the tenant so settled; and (b) For the purposes of determining the surplus area of any person under this section, any judgment, decree or order of a court or other authority obtained after the coming into force of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, and having the effect of diminishing the area of such persons which could have been declared as his surplus area shall be ignored.

The plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to the Zamindari on the death of Amarshah as an impartible estate, devolving by the rule of primogeniture and Pratapshah father of the plaintiffs was entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951. The defendants resisted the claim contending that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs were incorrect and that by the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram as Zamindar was not binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof, and the plaintiffs ' suit with regard to Malgu zari lands was not barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer. The Trial Court held that the order dated December 8, 1950 set up in favour of the defendants represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah; and that the will dated December 3, 1950, was genuine and the appellants were under the will entitled to compensation in regard thereto. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the judgment of the High Court was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari; (ii) that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of his power conferred by the Chanda Patent; and (iii) that section 14 of Act 1 Of 1951 did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. HELD: (i)(a) The order of compensation Officer under sub section (1) shall not be subject to any appeal or revision, but any party may institute a suit in the civil court to have the order set aside and the decision rendered by such court shall be binding on the Compensation officer, but subject to the result of such suit, if any, the Compensation Officers shall proceed to enquire summarily into the merits of such question and pass such orders as they thinks fit. [319 B] (b) The provisions of section 14 are extinguished. The right to property vesting in the Government by operation of section 3 is extinguished. Section 14 is enacted with a view to put an end to disputes with regard respect to the claims to proprietary rights which by 339 virtue of the notification issued under section 3 are extinguished, and if no suit is filed, the order becomes final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six, years after that date. [340 C D] (c) The right of property vesting under section 4 of Act I Of 1951 does not invest the Compensation Commis sion with jurisdiction to determine competing claims, of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting therein in the State by operation o section 3.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Gujarat Rent Control Act, 1958 provides that where there is a dispute as to the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if, before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3). The Bombay High Court took the view that the dispute as regards standard rent is to be raised within one month from the date of service of the notice on the tenant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: Section 12(4) of Act does not apply to a suit for recovery of rent whether with or without a claim for possession of the premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the ground that the rent is excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the court shall pass an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount of the rent as the Court considers to be reasonably due to the landlord, or at the option of the tenant an order directed him to pay to the landlords such amount as the court considers tobe reasonably due by the tenant under sub s.(2) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount thereof as the case may specify. The Bombay view is that in order to attract the applicability of section 12( 3)(a), there must be non existence of the dispute at the date when the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute, as contemplated in section 12 (2) (b) of that Act, and it is not enough to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. The tenant can claim protection from the operation of section12(3)(a) only if the tenant makes an applica tion within one months of the service of notice terminating tenancy by filing an application under sub sec.(2), before the expiration of the said period on one month of the date fixed for the hearing of the suit. A. No. A, No. C.A. No.. A. Nos. 859/71 and C. A No. 858/71 are therefore governed by the provisions contained in sections 12 (3) and 12(2)(a). The Gujarat High Court has taken a contrary view and held that the effect of sections 11 and 12 of the Act is to give the tenant a right to dispute the standard rent in the event of a suit and if the tenants raises a dispute in answer to a claim as to standard rent, it would be a dispute within the meaning of section 13(3), (a).

The respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company. L. G. Bash was appointed to vote and/or from time to time to appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the company, carried the right to vote. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondents company, the Aluminium Co., Ltd. appointed three temporary directors on board of Directors of the Respondent company and nominated a special/general proxy to votes for and upon behalf of its shareholders in breach of trust, nevertheless, as between them as shareholders and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest was vested in them, though as between themselves as shareholders they are the shareholders, and as such, have "a controlling interest" in the company. The respondent company was a director controlled company. In common parlance a person is said to have "A controlling interest", in a company when such a person acquires, by purchase or otherwise, the majority of the votes carrying shares in that company, for the control of the Company resides in the voting powers of its shareholder. In this sense, the directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a governing interest" and may even be accountable to their beneficiaries and may be brought to book for exercising their votes in breach Of trust, else, as long as his authority is not revoked, as far as the respondent is concerned, tile majority of its vote carrying shares are subject, directly or indirectly, to his will and ordering and, therefore, he cannot, applying either of the tests mentioned above, be said to had a controlling interest in the shares so held by L.G. Bash as agent of the aluminium Ltd., attends a general meeting of the directors authorising him to cast the votes of his principals. The High Court answered in the affirmative the question of law referred to it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (i) the directors had a control over their affairs at general meetings and as there was no room for doubt that the respondent ' company, which was then the appellant before the Appellate Tribunal, was a Director controlled company; (ii) the director of the appellant company nominated by the Aluminium Company Ltd. did not itself hold the majority shares which, on the contrary, were subject, indirectly or indirectly to his own will and directing, and, accordingly, he could not be said "a control interest" within the meaning of section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940; (iii) the High Court was right in holding that the directors did not themselves hold the minority of shares which on the facts found in the statement of the case were entirely different from the facts of the cases before it and that decision had no manner of application to the present case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i)(a) In order to have 'a controlling interests" the person or persons who hold the shares as trustees must have a beneficial interest in them when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority share which, under the articles, of association, of the companies, carry the right, to vote is vested in him, though he may be bound to cast votes according to the directions of his principal, the agent acquires no interest, legal or beneficial, in the shareholders and assuch have " a controlling interests " therein, no matter by what machinery or means that result has been effected. It is unfortunate that the last mentioned case was not brought to the notice of the High court before the judgment under appeal was delivered.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. The prayer made in the petition is for award of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of Suman Behra, for contravention of fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution and for violation of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights of the citizen. [608G H] 2.2 When the court molds the relief by granting "compensation" in proceedings under Article 32 or 226 of the constitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental Rights, it does so under the public law by way of penalising the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental right of the citizens. The payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making "monetary amends" under the Public Law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental freedoms of the Citizen. The compensation is in the nature of punitive damages awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the Private law in a suit instituted by a court of competent jurisdiction or/and persecute the offender under the penal law. [ 610A B] 2:3 The payment, of compensation, as exemplary damages, in proceedings for Article 32 by this Court or under Article 226 by the High Courts, for established infringement of the indefeasible right guaranteed by the Constitution, when that is the only practicable mode of redress available for the contravention made by the State or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, and enforcement of the fundamental Right is claimed by resort to Articles 32 and 226 of that Constitution, notwithstanding the right of a citizen to the remedy by way Of a civil suit or criminal proceedings. Of 610 course, relief in exercise of the power under Article32 or 226 would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of fundamental human rights of citizens and no other form of appropriate redressal by the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, is possible. The award of monetary compensation, if exemplary damages are awarded against wrong doers for the violation of their public law duties and are independent of their rights available under the civil law to the affected party where the courts found that grant of such relief was warranted.

The petitioners were convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, we would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to death. No such right can be claimed by the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to interview a condemned prisoner is 1186 willing to be interviewed. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for him to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview the prisoners jointly and for not more than one hour on the whole. There can be no doubt about this position because, for example rule 552A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview A prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. Taking an overall view of the matter, we do not see any reason why the petitioner could not be allowedto interview the two convicts Billa and Ranga. During the course of hearing of this petition, representatives of the Times of India, India Today, PTI and UNI also presented their applications asking for a similar permission. What we have said must hold good in their cases also and they, in our opinion, should be given the same facility of interviewing the prisoners as we are disposed to give to the petitioner in the main writ petition.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the appellant executed a surety bond in the sum of Rs. Goswami, District Judge, Agartala, his successors in office and assigns. By virtue of the powers conferred by the Tripura (Courts) order of 1950 which came into force on December 31, 1950, the District Judge transferred the mortgage suit to the court of the Subordinate Judge, West Tripura. On August 26, 1950 when the Receiver took possession of the estate on 22nd January, but since the security was not furnished, the Court directed on an application of the respondent that the Receiver should furnish the requisite security within the time allowed to him. On October 4, 1961 the appellant filed a suit for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956, but he also allowed the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner, Tripura on December 18, 1959. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) The Subordinate judge who tried the suit is incompetent to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant as he is neither the successor nor the assign of the District Court; and (2) Under the terms of the bond, the appellant is not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver can be executed against the appellant to the tune to which it rendered itself personally liable under the terms Of the bond. [360G H] (2)(a) The surety bond is a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Sub Judge. Therefore, by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate judge was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of the enforcement of the surety bonds as the District Magistrate himself. [361C D] (b) It is difficult to accept the contention that the receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea gardens. He was put in possession of his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea plantation was managed by the receiver economically and efficiently. The surety bonds would therefore cover the loss occasioned to the Tea garden due to the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties the appellant was liable to make good the loss suffered by the tea plant by the fire. [362E F] (c) It was impossible to accept that the Court owed no Duty or obligation on the Receiver because "successor in office" would mean successor of the district Judge in the post or office of theDistrict Judge who was seized of the case and who transferred it to the Subordinate Judges under the Tripura Act. [363D] (d) The bond is executed both for the purpose of the particular proceedings which were pending before a District Judge and on his transfer it was given retrospective operation with effect from January 22, 1950 being the date on which the Receiver had taken possession of that property including the tea grove. Therefore the order for recovery of damage obtained by a Receiver against the receiver can be made executed against him to the amount to which he has rendered himself personally liable in the manner provided for the execution of decrees.

Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1)(a) There was no offer by the tax payer to the Government of Madras, and no acceptance by the latter; the taxholder was under the Control order compelled to carrying out the direction of the controller and it had no volition in the matter. The tax payer contended that the supplies of sugar did not results in sales or were on account not exposure to sales Tax, because Steel products were sold pursuant to directions issued by the Iron & Steel Controller making under cl clause 5 was, therefore, not liable to sales taxation. [655 D] (b)(i) There is no contract between a licensed dealer and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the ambit of the definition in section 3(h). The taxholder contended that there was in the case then in hand mutual assent between the two parties, to the transaction of supply of coal. Wheat Procure ment (Levy) Order, upon the licensed dealer was imposed a liability to deliver half the quantity of wheat purchased by it every day commencing with the day of commencement and thereafter fifty per cent of the wheat daily procured or procured by him Every day beginning from the date when such time, as the state Government otherwise directs; Delivery of the goods is to take place at a future time or subject to some condition thereafter to be fulfilled, the contract is called an agreement to sell. It has to be given by the dealer to the Controller or to such other person as may be authorised by him in that behalf. If the liberty of contracts in relation to the fundamentals of the transaction is completely excluded a transaction of supplies pursuant to direction issued under a Conciliator Order may be regarded, as a sales.

The appellant, Abdul Latif Wahab Sheikh, was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. Though acquitted, he was not straightaway released from prison. The reasons are not clear to us from the record. Presumably he was required for release from prison on June 23, 1986 and the report of its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for the detention was required to be obtained within three months of the detention under article 22(4) of the Constitution. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the State submits that it is enough if the report is obtained within two months from the date of the second order of detention, where the earlier order is revoked and a subsequent order is made. The observation of the court to the extent that they go to support the contention of the appel lant, but we must say that in that case, the court was not confronted with the present situation at all. This implies that the question to which the Advisory Board has to apply its mind is whether on the date when the detention order was made, there was sufficient cause for detention of the person. That inquiry neces sary involves the consideration of the ques tion as to whether there was adequate cause for his detention. That enquiry nece ssary involves a consideration of (1) whether there were fresh facts, (2) whether the maximum period within which the detaining authority can on its own satisfaction detain a person is three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause justifying such detention; and (3) whether it is necessary to continue the detention of a person beyond the date on which its report or beyond the period of one month after the date fixed for the hearing of the case. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The observations of the Court to the effect that an order of preventive detention should have been made, knowing full well that there was no Advisory Board in existence to whom a reference could be made under the Act and whose report could be obtained as required by the Constitution must be read down so that it does not offend the mandate of article 22 (4) Of the Constitution that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention o f a person for a longer period than three months Unless the Advisory board has reported within the period specified in the order, place before the expiry of three month that there are in its view sufficient cause to justify such detention. If the report or the advisory Board is to be obtain ed within three weeks, it is no answer to say that the report though not obtained within four months, was obtained before the hearing on the case; and if the representation made by the detenu is required to he disposed of within a stipulated period, it would not answer to saying that the representation, though not made within three days, was disposed of before the hear ing of the cases. If a reference to an Advisory board is tobe made within two weeks, there is no question of extending the jurisdiction of the Advisory Boards to the consideration o f the question as to when it is required under the law against the same person subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh facts the maximum limit for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry period of 207 a period of 12 months from date of detention under the earlier detention order. If, however, the report made by such an Advisory body is to he obtained within six weeks, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it was within three month from the day of the first second order. [206G H; 206A B] 2.

The respondent was the father of the respondent. The award was endorsed and signed by both the parties. In the award, it was stated that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner and the respondent had agreed to such entrustment. It was further stated in the award that the whole responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on Shri Kantibhai Vaidya and that he has taken the responsibility. The endorsement reads, when translated in English as found by the High Court that the award is agreed to and binding upon both the party and that the full responsibility of Solving the disputes was entrusted on him and that it had taken the responsibilities. The respondent applied on 20th June, 1977 for filing the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). A notice consequent upon the filing of the Award was issued to the petitioner. It is clear from the narration of facts that the parties had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. In this connection, it may be useful to refer to the observations of this Court in Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, ; , where this Court observed that the validity of a decree could be challenged in execution proceedings only on the ground that the Court which passed the decree was lacking in inherent jurisdiction in the sense that it could not have seizing of the case because the subject matter was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the defendant was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matters of the suit or over the parties to it. In Seth Hira lal Patni, this Court held that they had perfect jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (namely, whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it. The Judicial Committee held that the conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the matter was entirely foreign to their jurisdiction or, that the party was dead when the suit has been instituted, or decree is passed or any some such ground which might have the impact of rendering of the court totally lacking in Jurisdiction in respect thereof. In that view of the matter, the High court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did.

The appellant instituted against his widow and sons O.S. No. 63 of 1954, asking for general partition of the coparcenary properties and for allotment to her of the properties conveyed by the two deeds. No 12/54, the decree for possession in respect of the property covered by exhibit A 2 being conditional on payment by the respondents of the value of improvements made by the appellant to the properties. HELD: (i) The transfers under Exs. A 1, A 2 and A 3 are invalid. Properly speaking, the past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for assignment. [114G H; 115A B] 2. It was not possible for the assignee to obtain revocation of the notices by the l.I.'C. as envisaged in clause(vii) of sub section (3). Section 29(2)(a) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 provides that where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that Schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of Limitation prescribed for any suits, appeals or applications by any special and local law (a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or special local law; and (b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply. The first limb of sub section (2) of section 29 is concerned with proceedings under special or general laws for which a period prescribed in the First Schedule has been provided therefor in the Second Schedule. Sub section (3) of that section provides that if any special, local law prescribing for any particular suit, appeals and applications a period different from that prescribed therefor, the provision contained in sub section(2) shall apply as if it were prescribed thereof in that schedule. The second limb of subsection (2), of section 30 is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under general or special laws for such suits, appeal and application by any local or special law which prescribes for such suit a different period of time limitation and that as in the 144 present case the First schedule has not prescribed any period for an appeal and that, therefore, cl. (a), applies to an appeal under the Representation of the People Act even though it does not fall under article 156 of the Limitation Act since a different periods of limitation were prescribed for it from that specified for an application in the first Schedule. Held, further, that the words "where any special law prescribes a period for which any suit or application is of a kind similar to one for which, a period Of limitation is prescribed in that sub section and for that purpose of deciding any period prescribed for such an appeal, appeal, or application by a special orLocal law" occurring in the second limb would include a suit or an appeal ' even though the it is not of a type for which no period of limitations is prescribed therefor. The words " where any Special or local Law prescribes for a suit, Appeal or application" in section 29(1) of Limitation Act are wide enough to cover suits under special and general laws but they do not include proceedings under ordinary law.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He questioned the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 702 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 declaring Plot nos. 701 & 702 in Town Area. The case of the appellant was that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a Bus stand under section 76 of the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') under which he purported to pass the impugned order. According to him, the power conferred on the State Government under section 68(2)(r) of the Act could be exercised only by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The High Court was of the opinion that section 76 had nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stands and the power to issue a notification fixing a bus Stand as a stage carriage stand was implied in section 68 (2)( r) of Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 76 of The Act confers wide powers on the District Magistrates 'to fix places for the bus stand and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the State Transport Authory as held by this Court in T.B. It only authorises the Regional transport Authority to take action immediately for determining any convenient place or places within the Town area of Baldev ( Mathura) as an bus stand. There is, however, no power conferred by section 68A(2) (r) to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop only at certain places for purposes of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specif ic provision in section68(2). The High court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned orde r dated 22.5.1986 passed by t he District Magistrate. [731C D] 2. Section 68(1)(r), which contained the provision relating to parking places and halting place had no application to a permanent bus stand which was a sort of radiating centre of all the bus traffic in the town. The Municipal Council contended before this Court that section76 of the . Act conferred wide powers upon the District Commis sioner to fix the places for bus stand as a Stage carriage stand and that could be done only under section68 (2)(r) Of the Act. Such a power should be given specifically by the statute and that the power of compel persons In charge of Motor Vehicles to stop even at certain place for the pur pose of taking over or setting up passengers was not a purpose for eign to the control of transport vehicles ' which was gov erned by Chapter IV of the , Act and, therefore the order passed under that provision was open to revision under section 64A by the state Transport Authority. Such power should also be given expressly by the statutes and that such power should have been given specifically in the statute. [758E F] 3. The Regional Transport Authori trate could not be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act and that would be done even under section 69(2), (r). [758G H] 4. Section 78 of the is confined to the question of determination of parking places, halting places etc., which are neither the same nor the bus stands where can only he notified by Regional Transport authori ty.

In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) if any person contravenes any order made under section 3(a) he shall be punishable (i) in the ease of an order made with reference to clause (h) or clause (i), of sub section (2) of that section, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and shall also be liable to fine; and (ii) in any other case, with fine. HELD: (1) There was no export of rice within the meaning of Para 2(a). It follows therefore that there has been no export or attempt on the part of the appellants and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt to committing it. Sir James Stephen, in his Digest of Criminal Law, article 50 defines an attempt as follows: " 'an act done with intent to commit that crime, or forming part of a series of acts which would constitute its actual commission if it were not interrupted. The Sassoons had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which had been paid by the Companies to the transferees and were, therefore, liable to tax in respect of the same. The Income Tax Officer held that the Sassoon became entitled on the very date of the respective assignments to a proportionate share of the year 's remuneration for the Managing Agents commission which accrued to them during the broken period could certainly be said to have accrued to the Sassoonons, during the chargeable accounting period. On appeal by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that in any event, what was transferred by the Sas Soons to the respective transferees were merely expectations of earning commission and not any part or of the commission actually earned by them or which had accrued to it under the terms of the managing Agency Agreements. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that in computing the taxable income of the assignee, can it reasonably be said that the remuneration for his entire year is the income which has accrued to him during the taxable accounting period; and (2) that if so far as in the present case, the Managing Agent had been referred to as service and the commission therefor as their taxable income, then and there, and did not cease to be such notwithstanding the assignment thereof. HELD: (i) The right of the assignor to receive the entire remuneration does not depend on any specific term between the assignors and the assignee but on the fact that what was transfer is an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that falls due after the date of assignment. It may be mentioned in this context that clauses I and 3 of the said Managing Agency Agreement show that the employer is to be responsible only to the assignee for the payment of the entire year ''s remuneration, but by the very terms of which the assignee becomes the Managing agent as if his name had been inserted in the Managing agency Agreement from the beginning, and that whoever satisfies the description of the deceased Managing Agent at the time when the commission for the year became due, is also the person entitled to the amount by way of remuneration not, as per this argument by virtue of any mutual arrangement between the assignee and the transferee, either as part of his deed of transfer or independent thereof. The right to receive a entire remuneration did not depend upon any specific terms between the assignmentor and the transferees, but on that fact it may be that in the normal run of events the contract for remuneration under the Managing Agencies Agreement is an indivisible contract for a whole year's work, this clause necessarily implied divisibility of contract and the remuneration in the year of assignment since the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal Mill Company. [372 E F] (ii) It may also be mentioned that though any mere clause in the managing agency Agreement that the employee is to he responsible only for the payments of the whole year ' his remuneration was not by itself enough to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to him the remuneration of the years, such a right may arise by virtue Of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferor either as Part of the deed of assignment or independent thereto.
